questions.q: Why does the lesson say tool schemas are 'context,' not just metadata for developers?
options: Because every offered tool's schema is sent as part of the context window on every call, and the model reads the description to decide when and how to call it
Because tool schemas are never actually sent to the model
Because tool schemas replace the system prompt entirely
Because only the first tool offered counts as context
questions.explain: Tool definitions are part of what's sent to the model on every call, whether or not that tool is used, and the model reads the description text to decide whether and how to call it.

questions.q: What is the main problem with the vague tool description "Gets order info." with a parameter just called "id"?
options: It uses too many tokens compared to a detailed version
It is not valid JSON
It costs roughly the same tokens as a precise description but gives the model far less information about when to call it and what format "id" expects
It cannot be parsed by any model
questions.explain: The lesson frames a vague description as the worst combination: similar token cost to a precise one, but much less useful information for the model.

questions.q: In the improved tool definition, what detail tells the model the tool is safe to call without risking an unintended side effect?
options: The tool's name alone
The description stating it is a read-only lookup
The fact that it has a required parameter
The use of the word "order" in the name
questions.explain: The improved description explicitly states the tool is a read-only lookup, which tells the model it won't change data — distinct from the vague version, which never addresses this.

questions.q: Which of the four rules in this lesson addresses parameter definitions specifically?
options: Keep it short
Say what it does and when
State constraints and side effects
Describe parameters precisely — format, units, valid values, not just the type
questions.explain: The second rule specifically targets parameter descriptions, calling for format, units, or valid values rather than just a bare type like "string."

questions.q: Why does the lesson say precision and brevity usually aren't in tension when writing a tool description?
options: Because a precise description is usually also a short one, while a vague one often runs long without saying anything specific
Because precise descriptions are always written in a different language
Because brevity is more important than precision in all cases
Because tool descriptions are never read by the model, only by developers
questions.explain: The lesson notes that being specific (trigger condition, parameter format) tends to produce concise text, while vague descriptions often ramble without adding useful detail.
